Figure 1:Action-only conditioning leaves the scene’s response to the video model.(a) A simulator predicts how scene points respond, so the video model mainly renders this response.
(b) Two DROID test clips: objects respond wrongly with action-only conditioning (robot render; red) but not with the proxy (green).

Figure 2:The proxy carries the object’s response into the video.Test clips (Wan2.2,t=1.3t=1.3s, cropped); the left column shows the simulated point trajectories on the first frame.
Without point dynamics, a carried cup stays on the tray, a cloth slides off the chair and a lifted towel bunches up (red); with the proxy, the objects respond as in the real video (green).

Figure 3:The video follows the simulation.Object motion error on the DROID test set when the simulator is swapped (a) or its output perturbed (b) at test time, with the trained renderer fixed.
Dots left of the vertical lines (robot render only) are better.

Figure 4:Editing the simulated motion steers the video.In this successful example, the simulated motion of the cloth is frozen or doubled at test time, with the robot and the rest of the scene unchanged (Wan2.2).
Left: the (edited) point trajectories.

Figure 5:The proxy carries the bag’s response into the real-robot video.Test clips (Wan2.2,t=1.3t=1.3s, cropped); the left column shows the simulated trajectories on the first frame.
Without point dynamics, the bag is not unfolded, does not swing when carried, or after a handover hangs from the wrong arm or appears twice (red); with the proxy, it responds as in the real video (green).
